Complex surfaces with many algebraic structures
Anna Abasheva, Rodion D´eev
Abstract
We ﬁnd new examples of complex surfaces with countably many non-isomorphic
algebraic structures. Here is one such example: take an elliptic curve E in P2 and blow
up nine general points on E. Then the complement M of the strict transform of E in the
blow-up has countably many algebraic structures. Moreover, each algebraic structure
comes from an embedding of M into a blow-up of P2 in nine points lying on an elliptic
curve F ̸≃E. We classify algebraic structures on M using a Hopf transform: a way of
constructing a new surface by cutting out an elliptic curve and pasting a diﬀerent one.
Next, we introduce the notion of an analytic K-theory of varieties. Manipulations
with the example above lead us to prove that classes of all elliptic curves in this K-theory
coincide. To put in another way, all motivic measures on complex algebraic varieties
that take equal values on biholomorphic varieties do not distinguish elliptic curves.

2.1
Analytic compactiﬁcations
Deﬁnition 2.1.1. Let M be a non-compact complex surface. A pair (S, C) of a smooth
compact complex surface S and (possibly singular) curve C ⊂S is called an analytic compact-
iﬁcation or just a compactiﬁcation of M if S −C is biholomorphic to M. A compactiﬁcation
is called minimal if none of the curves in the support of C are exceptional.
The following classiﬁcation theorem is due to Enoki [Eno82, Theorem C-I0].
Theorem 2.1.2. Let Tot(L) be the total space of a line bundle L of degree zero over an
elliptic curve E. Then every minimal compactiﬁcation (S, C) of M is of the following form:
1. S ∼= P(O ⊕L) is a P1-bundle over an elliptic curve; C is its section, and (C)2 = 0.
2. S is a Hopf surface (Deﬁnition 2.2.1), and C is an elliptic curve.
If L is non-torsion, the set of Hopf surfaces compactifying Tot(L) is countable, as we will
see in Theorem 2.3.2. For now, let us note that all such compactiﬁcations contain at least
two elliptic curves.
2.2
Hopf surfaces
Deﬁnition 2.2.1. [Kod66, Sect. 10] A Hopf surface is a compact complex surface whose
universal cover is C2 −{0}. A Hopf surface is called primary if its fundamental group is Z,
otherwise it is called secondary.
2.2.2. All Hopf surfaces are non-K¨ahler. By [Kod66, Sect. 10, p. 695] every primary Hopf
surface X is biholomorphic to a quotient C2 −{0}/Γ where Γ is either a linear diagonal
operator or of the form
Γ(x, y) = (αnx + yn, αy).
In the second case, a Hopf surface has only one irreducible curve: the image of the x-axis.
Therefore, such surfaces do not arise as compactiﬁcations of Tot(L).
2.2.3. Let us study the case when Γ = diag(λ, µ). In order for C2 −{0}/Γ to be compact,
the absolute values of the eigenvalues must be either both greater than one or both less than
one. By replacing Γ with Γ−1 if necessary, we may assume the latter.
Deﬁnition 2.2.4. A diagonal Hopf surface is C2 −{0}/ diag(λ, µ) for |λ| < 1, |µ| < 1. We
will denote it by H(λ, µ)
2.2.5. One can show that two Hopf surfaces H(λ, µ) and H(λ′, µ′) are isomorphic if and
only if λ = λ′ and µ = µ′ (up to a permutation). All automorphisms of H(λ, µ) are induced
by a linear diagonal automorphism of C2.

2.2.6. If λn = µm for some non-zero integers n and m then H(λ, µ) is an elliptic surface
with smooth but possibly non-reduced ﬁbers [BHPVdV15, Ch. V, Prop. 18.2]. All elliptic
curves in X are ﬁbers, hence their normal bundles are torsion. Such a surface cannot be a
compactiﬁcation of Tot(L) for a non-torsion line bundle L.
When λn ̸= µm for any pair of non-zero integers the surface H(λ, µ) contains exactly two
irreducible curves [BHPVdV15, Ch. V, Prop. 18.2]. They are the images of the axes under
the quotient map and are isomorphic to Eλ := C∗/λ and Eµ := C∗/µ. They have both
square zero.
The complement to Eµ in H(λ, µ) is C∗× C/ diag(λ, µ). It is the total space of a line
bundle over Eλ, and the map to Eλ is the projection to the ﬁrst coordinate.
